en: The Scripture on the Eleven Contemplations Spoken by the Buddha for Mindfully Recollecting the Tathāgata, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was together with a great assembly of two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should contemplate the Tathāgata by means of eleven reflections; having contemplated him, you should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward the Tathāgata.”
What are the eleven? First, purity of ethical conduct and intention.
Second, perfection of dignified demeanor.
Third, the faculties are not confused.
Fourth, the mind of faith is undisturbed.
Fifth, there is always a courageous and resolute intention.
Sixth, not regarding further suffering or pleasure as a cause for anxiety;
seventh, the mind being free from forgetfulness;
eighth, the presence of tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Ninth, the mind of samādhi is without rest.
Tenth, the mind of wisdom is immeasurable.
Eleventh, one never tires of contemplating the Buddha.

In this way, a bhikṣu should contemplate the Tathāgata by means of these eleven reflections. Having contemplated the Tathāgata, he should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward the Tathāgata; this is called a bhikṣu practicing the recollection of the Buddha among the bhikṣus.
That bhikṣu, having already practiced the recollection of the Buddha, shall seek one of the two fruits and attain mastery in the present life, becoming an anāgāmin without remainder.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one draws near to, extensively disseminates, practices, and perfects the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness (maitrī-cetovimukti), thereby attaining the full completion of its arising, there will then be eleven rewards and eleven fruits."
What are these eleven? One sleeps in peace and awakens in peace;

one does not see evil dreams; one is protected by devas; one is loved by humans; one is respected by non-humans; one is not harmed by poison; one is not harmed by weapons; one does not perish by fire or water; one does not suffer legal punishment; and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is reborn in a good destination, in the Brahma Heaven.
One will swiftly attain agility regarding all wholesome dharmas, and through wisdom, one will be able to exhaust all taints (*āsrava*). O Bhikṣu!

When the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness is cultivated, practiced extensively, developed through cultivation, and brought to fulfillment, eleven qualities will arise as its accompaniments. These are the eleven dharmas that shall be present.
"Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means for liberation through a mind of loving-kindness; thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Eleven Contemplations Spoken by the Buddha for Recollecting the Tathāgata.
